overview:
Three centuries of rule began with a rebel from nothing. Zhu Yuanzhang, orphaned by famine and once a begging monk, rose through the anti-Mongol revolts of the mid-fourteenth century, destroyed his rivals, and in 1368 drove the Yuan court back onto the steppe, proclaiming himself the Hongwu emperor with his capital at Nanjing. What he built was deliberately austere and deeply suspicious: a codified legal order, a self-supporting hereditary garrison system, villages organized for tax and labor registration, and periodic purges of the officials around him that killed on a scale historians estimate in the tens of thousands. His son Zhu Di seized the throne from a nephew in a civil war ending in 1402 and reigned as the Yongle emperor, in effect refounding the dynasty on grander terms — moving the capital north to Beijing, raising the Forbidden City there between roughly 1407 and 1420, campaigning into Mongolia, and dispatching the eunuch admiral Zheng He on seven enormous fleets that reached Southeast Asia, India, Arabia, and the East African coast before the court abandoned them as ruinously expensive.

The dynasty that followed was less outward-facing but far from closed. Official bans on private sea trade pushed commerce into smuggling and fed the mixed Chinese-Japanese piracy of the sixteenth-century coast, yet Chinese silk and Jingdezhen blue-and-white porcelain still moved across the world, and from the 1570s Spanish galleons carried American silver from Potosí through Manila into an economy that had come to run on the metal. Population climbed steeply, cities and commercial printing flourished, vernacular novels and illustrated books found readers well below the scholar-official elite, and the Wang Yangming school unsettled orthodox Confucian teaching from within. Defense stayed the permanent anxiety. The 1449 Tumu crisis, in which Mongols captured a reigning emperor, was the humiliation behind the long program of brick-and-stone wall-building along the northern frontier that produced most of what visitors now call the Great Wall.

The end came from several directions at once. The long Wanli reign drained the treasury on frontier wars, including the costly defense of Korea against Hideyoshi's invasions in the 1590s, while the emperor withdrew from governing and factional and eunuch politics hardened at court. In the 1630s and 1640s the coldest stretch of the Little Ice Age brought failed harvests, and disruptions to the silver flow squeezed a monetized economy that had no cushion; famine, epidemic disease, and unpaid soldiers turned into mass rebellion. In 1644 the rebel Li Zicheng entered Beijing and the Chongzhen emperor hanged himself; a Ming general opened the passes to the Manchus, who took the capital for their own Qing dynasty. Ming claimants held out in the south until the early 1660s.
significance: The Ming left the physical and institutional shape of China that later centuries inherited: Beijing as capital, the Forbidden City, the masonry Great Wall, and a civil service recruited by examination on a scale that made bureaucratic government the normal condition of the largest state on earth. Its factories and looms also made it one hinge of the first genuinely global economy — Chinese demand for silver is what gave American mines their value, and Chinese porcelain set a standard that European potters spent two centuries trying to imitate. And its collapse is one of the most studied cases anywhere of how climate shock, fiscal strain, and monetary dependence on a distant supply can compound into the fall of a seemingly secure regime.
coverage: The dataset holds no events at all for this story, so nothing here comes from the map's own records; this is written from general reference sources — Wikipedia's survey article and the Smithsonian's museum overview — rather than from specialist scholarship. The Ming is unusually well documented by pre-modern standards, with voluminous official histories, veritable records, and gazetteers, but those sources are court-centered and moralizing: they say much about emperors and officials and comparatively little about peasants, women, and non-Han peoples on the frontiers. Specific numbers should be treated as estimates — population figures, the death tolls of Hongwu's purges, and the tonnage and reach of Zheng He's ships are all debated, and the fleets' records were partly destroyed by later officials hostile to the voyages. The relative weight of climate, silver, taxation, and politics in the dynasty's fall remains actively contested.
